1121.quote_or_event: “My Dear Lord and Master, my Friend, speaks so sweetly.”
1121.explanation: In a hymn of the bride-soul, Guru Arjan calls the Lord a friend (sajan) whose every word is sweet, using the Punjabi diminutive 'mith bolarha', the sweet-speaking one.
1121.tie_back: As the Kural's lover tastes milk and honey in the mouth of his soft-spoken beloved, the Guru delights in the sweetness of the Beloved's speech.
1121.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 784, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1121._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on the sweetness of the beloved's speech, but the love is spiritual, for God as Friend, not romantic, and the Kural's image is of the mouth rather than the words.

1122.quote_or_event: “O mind, love the Lord, as the lotus loves the water.”
1122.explanation: Guru Nanak asks for a love so bound to the Lord that, like the lotus that cannot live apart from water, the soul draws its very life from Him.
1122.tie_back: The Kural's bond of body and life (udambu and uyir) finds its Sikh counterpart in the lotus and the water, a pairing in which one cannot survive without the other.
1122.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 59, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1122._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a strong image of inseparable union, though it describes the soul's spiritual love for God rather than human lovers, and uses lotus and water instead of body and life.

1123.quote_or_event: “The crows have searched my skeleton, and eaten all my flesh. But please do not touch these eyes; I hope to see my Lord.”
1123.explanation: Sheikh Farid, wasted by longing, gives up his whole body to the crows but keeps his two eyes back, because they are reserved for the sight of the Beloved.
1123.tie_back: Like the Kural's lover who orders even the little image in his pupil to leave so that the eye holds only his beloved, Farid keeps his eyes for the Beloved alone.
1123.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 91) (BaniDB English translation)
1123._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB, whose database gives the Sant Singh Khalsa reading for the first line but only its own BaniDB English for the second, so the BaniDB translation is named; a striking parallel of eyes kept for the beloved, though the longing is spiritual, for God.

1124.quote_or_event: “Chanting it, I live; forgetting it, I die.”
1124.explanation: In the evening prayer So Dar (Rehras), Guru Nanak says that remembering the Name is life itself and that forgetting it is a kind of death.
1124.tie_back: The Kural's beloved is life when present and death when she leaves, exactly the two poles Guru Nanak sets between remembering and forgetting the Beloved.
1124.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 9, So Dar (Rehras), Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1124._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a near one-to-one match of the living/dying antithesis, with the beloved being the divine Name rather than a human lover.

1125.quote_or_event: “They do not forget, even for an instant, the Support of the breath of life. They live by constantly meditating on Him, O Nanak.”
1125.explanation: Guru Arjan describes devotees who never let the Beloved slip from mind, so that unbroken remembrance (simran) becomes the very thing they live by.
1125.tie_back: The Kural's lover never forgets his beloved's qualities and so never needs to recall them; Gurbani's devotees likewise never forget, even for an instant.
1125.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 80, Sri Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1125._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a strong fit on ceaseless remembrance, though it lacks the Kural's witty paradox that one cannot remember what one never forgets, and the object of love is God.

1126.quote_or_event: “Kabeer: with my eyes, I see You, Lord; with my ears, I hear Your Name.”
1126.explanation: Bhagat Kabir asks that his eyes behold only the Lord, so that the Beloved fills his sight wherever he looks.
1126.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says her lover never leaves her eyes; Kabir likewise keeps the Beloved always before his eyes.
1126.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1370, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1126._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a reasonable but partial fit on the beloved dwelling in the eyes, without the Kural's conceit that he is too subtle to be hurt by blinking, and the love is for God.

1127.quote_or_event: “I have applied the healing ointment of spiritual wisdom to my eyes; the Naam, the Name of the Lord, is my food. These are all my decorations.”
1127.explanation: Guru Arjan's bride-soul replaces the usual kohl (anjan) and adornments with the Guru's wisdom and the Name, so that her eyes are made ready only for the Beloved.
1127.tie_back: The Kural's heroine refuses kohl so as not to hide the lover dwelling in her eyes; the Sikh bride-soul sets aside ordinary kohl for the 'ointment of wisdom' that reveals the Lord.
1127.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 542, Raag Bihaagraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1127._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a strong fit on eye-ointment and the beloved, though the logic differs (spiritual kohl revealing God rather than refusing kohl to keep the lover visible) and the love is spiritual, not romantic.

1128.quote_or_event: “O Baba, the pleasures of other foods are false. Eating them, the body is ruined, and wickedness and corruption enter into the mind.”
1128.explanation: Guru Nanak warns against foods eaten for pleasure that harm the body and disturb the mind, setting restraint in eating within a life centred on the Lord.
1128.tie_back: The Kural's heroine avoids hot food so as not to scorch the lover in her heart; Guru Nanak likewise guards what he eats for the sake of what dwells within the mind.
1128.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1128._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a next-best match only: it shares restraint in food for an inward reason, but has nothing of the Kural's playful conceit of a lover burnt by hot food in the heart.

1129.quote_or_event: “Night and day, I utter, "Pri-a, Pri-a - Beloved, Beloved" with my mouth. I cannot sleep, even for an instant; I remain awake and aware.”
1129.explanation: Guru Arjan voices the bride-soul who stays wakeful through the night, calling out to the Beloved and refusing the sleep that would take Him from her.
1129.tie_back: The Kural's heroine will not close her eyes lest her lover be hidden; the Sikh bride-soul likewise stays awake without blinking into sleep, held by her Beloved.
1129.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1203, Raag Saarang, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1129._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a good fit on loving sleeplessness, but it lacks the Kural's twist of the town wrongly calling the lover unloving, and the love is spiritual.

1130.quote_or_event: “Why do you go looking for Him in the forest? Although he is unattached, he dwells everywhere. He is always with you as your companion.”
1130.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur tells seekers who think the Lord is far away and must be sought in the wilderness that He already dwells with them, within.
1130.tie_back: The town in the Kural says the lover lives far away, while the heroine knows he dwells rejoicing in her heart; Gurbani answers those who think the Beloved distant with the same certainty that He is always near.
1130.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 684, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1130._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a strong fit on 'others think him far, but he dwells within me', with the Beloved being God rather than a human lover.
